title: Transient and universal regimes in quantum reaction-transport kinetics
abstract: Quantum reaction-transport systems consist of coherently propagating particles that irreversibly react upon encounter. Their relaxation is commonly classified as reaction-limited or transport-limited, depending on the relative timescales of reaction and particle transport. We show that this expectation fails in low dimensions by studying the quantum binary annihilation, $A+A \to \emptyset$, where reaction processes acquire singular fluctuation corrections below the upper critical dimension $D_c=2$. Consequently, fluctuations dominate the asymptotic kinetics for $D<2$. In one dimension, they render mean-field relaxation transient and drive the system toward a transport-limited regime with $n\sim t^{-1/2}$, governed by a quantum-Zeno scale even for arbitrarily weak loss. At $D=2$, the kinetics acquires logarithmic corrections, whereas above two dimensions mean-field scaling is asymptotically restored. At and below the upper critical dimension, mean-field behavior can nevertheless persist over parametrically long crossover times before the asymptotic fluctuation-dominated regime emerges. We also show that the same fluctuations generate effective elastic collisions despite the absence of microscopic coherent interactions. In $D>1$, these collisions redistribute momentum populations and are parametrically faster than losses in the transport-limited regime, allowing the system to approach a quasi-stationary thermal state.
summary: This work analyzes the long-time kinetics of quantum systems undergoing irreversible reactions, showing that the decay rate of particle density is highly sensitive to the spatial dimension D. The results reveal a dimensional crossover, where fluctuations dominate below D=2, leading to different power-law decays compared to the mean-field predictions for D>2.
main_problem: The paper investigates the universal long-time kinetic behavior of quantum reaction-transport systems, specifically determining how particle density decays in different spatial dimensions.
main_result: The asymptotic decay rate of particle density depends critically on the spatial dimension D, showing $n \sim t^{-1/2}$ in 1D, logarithmic corrections in 2D, and mean-field $n \sim t^{-1}$ for $D>2$.
method: The analysis employs Keldysh field theory and kinetic theory, deriving equations of motion for momentum occupations by treating the system's evolution as a competition between reaction losses and elastic collisions.
model_or_system: The system models quantum reaction-transport kinetics using quantum binary annihilation ($A+A 	o \emptyset$) governed by a quantum master equation. The dynamics are analyzed via a kinetic equation for momentum occupations $n_k = \langle \psi_k^\dagger \psi_k angle$.
key_observables: Particle density $n(t)$, temperature $T(t)$, momentum distribution width $Q(t)$, and the renormalized reaction vertex $T(k, p)$.
important_parameters: Spatial dimension $D$, loss strength $\Gamma$, and the upper critical dimension $D_c=2$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the T-matrix approximation for diagrammatic resummation and often involves retaining terms up to quadratic order in occupations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the kinetic-regime diagram showing dependence on D and loss strength, and diagrammatic representations of the T-matrix derivation for pair annihilation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the general kinetic framework, deriving the kinetic equation for momentum occupations, and then analyzing the asymptotic limits separately for $D=1$, $D=2$, and $D>2$ to determine the universal scaling laws.
why_interesting: The dimensional crossover behavior ($D<2$ vs $D>2$) and the emergence of effective thermalization mechanisms from purely dissipative quantum processes are highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and open quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic kinetic-regime diagram as a function of spatial dimension D and loss strength Γ/J. In D = 1, the asymptotic dynamics is transport-limited with n ∼t−1/2, although weak loss can produce a long transient reaction- limited regime. D = 2 is marginal, with n ∼(ln t)/t, while for D > 2 the mean-field decay n ∼t−1 is asymptotically restored. At strong loss and D > 1, emergent elastic collisions can rapidly redistribute particles and establish a quasi-stationary thermal state.
FIG. 3. (a) Self-consistent diagrammatic equation for the T- matrix. (b) Boson self-energy in terms of the T-matrix.

FIG. 4. (a) Time evolution of the momentum distribution normalized by the average density in one dimension for J = Γ. Higher-momentum modes decay more rapidly, causing the surviving population to concentrate near k = 0. (b) Density evolution for different hopping strengths. The asymptotic decay follows n ∼t−1/2 for all J/Γ, while for strong hopping a parametrically long transient mean-field regime n ∼t−1 can precede the asymptotic scaling.
